title: 01. Fundamentals & Trade-offs: Durability
summary: Durability is the property that once data has been acknowledged as written, it persists despite hardware failures, power loss, software crashes, or network partitions, for as long as the data is intended to be retained.
objectives: What is the difference between durability and availability? Give an example of each.
Explain replication factor (RF) and quorum writes. Why does RF=3 with QUORUM give strong durability?
Compare replication vs erasure coding. When does each win?
What is a silent data corruption, and how do storage systems defend against it?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Durability is the property that once data has been acknowledged as written, it persists despite hardware failures, power loss, software crashes, or network partitions, for as long as the data is intended to be retained.

Durability is the most underappreciated non-functional requirement in system design because, until it fails, it is invisible. Availability failures are loud — users see a 500 page and complain immediately. Latency failures are also loud — users see a spinner and abandon. Durability failures are silent — a file written in 2019 may not be readable in 2024 because three disks silently rotted and the replicas were never reconciled. By the time anyone notices, the data is gone forever, with no recovery path. This is why storage systems invest enormous engineering in durability: AWS S3 Standard is designed for 99.999999999% (eleven nines) durability over a year, meaning that if you store 10,000 objects, you should expect to lose one every 10 million years. That number is not marketing — it is a math result from erasure coding plus cross-region replication plus continuous integrity scrubbing.

Durability is achieved through two complementary mechanisms: redundancy and verification. Redundancy means storing each piece of data in multiple places so that no single failure (or any plausible combination of failures) can destroy it. The simplest form is replication: store N identical copies on N independent disks or nodes. Cassandra uses a default replication factor (RF) of 3, meaning every row lives on three nodes; as long as one of those three survives, the data survives. Replication is easy to reason about but storage-inefficient — RF=3 triples your storage cost. The alternative is erasure coding: split each object into k data chunks plus m parity chunks (e.g., 10+4), and store the 14 chunks across 14 failure domains. You can lose any 4 of the 14 and still reconstruct the data. The storage overhead drops from 3x (RF=3) to 1.4x (10+4 erasure), a massive saving at scale. AWS S3, Google Cloud Storage, and Azure Blob all use erasure coding internally for exactly this reason.

Quorum writes are the second mechanism, and they matter for strong durability guarantees. In a replicated system with RF=N, a write can be acknowledged after W replicas confirm it, where W is the write quorum. If W=N, every replica must ack before the write is acknowledged — maximum durability, but slowest (the write is only as fast as the slowest replica) and most fragile (one unreachable replica blocks all writes). If W=1, the write is acknowledged as soon as one replica has it — fastest, but if that replica crashes before the write propagates, the data is lost. The common compromise for durability-focused workloads is W=majority: in RF=3, that means W=2. As long as any two of the three replicas have the write, the data survives any single-node failure. Cassandra and Dynamo use this tunable quorum model, letting operators trade durability vs latency at the per-request level. The pitfall: a quorum write does not guarantee that *all* replicas have the data — only that a majority does. If the majority replica fails immediately after acking and the minority hasn't yet received the write, a careful read path is needed to avoid reading stale data.

The classic real-world example of durability engineering is AWS S3. S3 Standard is designed for 11 nines of durability over a year. The math: with RF=3 across three Availability Zones, the probability of losing an object is roughly (independent_disk_failure_rate)^3, which is already astronomically low. But S3 does not actually use RF=3 internally — it uses erasure coding within each AZ (storing data plus parity across many disks) plus cross-AZ replication plus a background scrubber that continuously reads every object, computes its checksum, and repairs any bit rot. The scrubber is critical because disks fail silently — they return data that looks fine but is corrupted by bit rot, controller bugs, or firmware issues. Without active verification, the system would accumulate silent corruption until a read fails years later. This is why S3's published durability number assumes active scrubbing, not just redundancy.

A second instructive example is Cassandra's tunable consistency. A Cassandra cluster with RF=3 can be configured at the request level: write with consistency level ONE (ack after one replica), QUORUM (ack after two of three), or ALL (ack after all three). For a banking ledger, you'd use QUORUM or ALL writes and QUORUM reads — strong durability, slightly higher latency. For a metrics pipeline that can tolerate occasional loss, ONE writes are fine and dramatically faster. The trade-off is explicit and per-request: more replicas acked = more durable but slower; fewer = faster but riskier. Netflix uses Cassandra heavily for their viewing-history store, configured with LOCAL_QUORUM writes to balance durability against cross-region latency. They accept that a single AZ failure will not lose data, but they also accept that a regional catastrophe could lose data not yet replicated cross-region — and they manage that residual risk with backup snapshots.

The pitfall that catches every team eventually is conflating durability with consistency or availability. A system can be perfectly durable (every acknowledged write survives forever) and still be unavailable (the system is down so no new writes can be acknowledged) or inconsistent (different replicas return different versions of an object during a partition). Conversely, a system can be highly available but have weak durability — for example, an async-replication primary/secondary database where the primary accepts writes, acks to the client, and then replicates to the secondary in the background; if the primary crashes before replication completes, the write is lost even though the client was told it succeeded. This is the famous "data loss on failover" scenario that bites every team using async replication without understanding the durability window. The fix is synchronous replication (the primary waits for the secondary to ack before acking the client), which trades latency for durability.

Durability connects to every other system design concept. It is constrained by cost — more replicas and more parity means more storage. It interacts with availability — a write that must wait for all replicas is slower and blocks more easily. It interacts with latency — synchronous replication adds network round-trips to every write. It interacts with consistency — quorum reads with quorum writes give strong consistency but cost latency. It interacts with fault tolerance — a system that loses data on a single failure is not fault-tolerant. Senior engineers treat durability as a probability, not a binary: "this workload tolerates a 1-in-10^9 chance of data loss per year" is a meaningful statement, while "this data is 100% durable" is fiction. Designing for the right durability level per workload — and being explicit about the residual risk — is the mark of a mature storage system.

sections.title: Visual Explanation
sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Client Write Request] --> B[Coordinator Node] B --> C[Replicate to N nodes
RF=3] C --> D1[Node 1: ack] C --> D2[Node 2: ack] C --> D3[Node 3: ack] D1 --> E{Tally acks} D2 --> E D3 --> E E -- "< W acks" --> F[Reject write
or retry] E -- ">= W acks" --> G[Acknowledge to client] G --> H[Write is durable
survives loss of N-W+1 nodes] H --> I[Background repair
syncs late replicas] ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` +-------------+ | Coordinator | +------+------+ | +--------------+--------------+ | | | v v v +---------+ +---------+ +---------+ | Node 1 | | Node 2 | | Node 3 | | acks | | acks | | slow... | +---------+ +---------+ +---------+ \ / | \ / | v v v W=2 reached (QUORUM) eventually acks | | v v +-----------+ background | ack client| repair syncs +-----------+ node 3 ``` ### Walkthrough 1. The client sends a write to a coordinator node (chosen by hash partition or load balancer). The coordinator is responsible for replicating the write to all replicas of that data. 2. The coordinator sends the write to all N replicas in parallel (RF=3 in the example). Each replica persists the write locally — typically to an append-only commit log first, then to its memtable or storage engine. 3. Each replica sends an acknowledgment once it has durably persisted the write (flushed to disk, fsync'd). The coordinator counts acks. 4. The coordinator compares ack count to the configured write quorum W. If W=2 (QUORUM with RF=3), it acks the client as soon as two replicas have the write — even if the third is still pending. 5. A background repair process (read-repair in Cassandra, anti-entropy in Dynamo, or the scrubber in S3) periodically ensures all replicas converge. If a replica was down during the write, it is brought up to date when it returns.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
"""
Durability simulator: compare replication factor vs erasure coding
on storage overhead and probability of data loss.
"""
import math
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class ReplicationConfig:
    rf: int  # replication factor (e.g., 3)

    def storage_overhead(self) -> float:
        # Every byte is stored RF times -> overhead = RF
        return float(self.rf)

    def fault_tolerance(self) -> int:
        # Can tolerate losing RF-1 replicas before data is lost
        return self.rf - 1

    def annual_data_loss_probability(self, disk_annual_failure_rate: float) -> float:
        # Independent failures of all RF replicas simultaneously
        # P(loss) ~= p^RF (assuming correlated failures negligible)
        p = disk_annual_failure_rate
        return p ** self.rf

@dataclass
class ErasureCodingConfig:
    k: int  # data chunks
    m: int  # parity chunks

    def storage_overhead(self) -> float:
        # Total stored = (k + m) chunks for k chunks of data
        # Overhead = (k + m) / k
        return (self.k + self.m) / self.k

    def fault_tolerance(self) -> int:
        # Can tolerate losing any m chunks
        return self.m

    def annual_data_loss_probability(self, chunk_annual_failure_rate: float,
                                     correlated_failure_rate: float = 1e-6) -> float:
        # P(loss) = P(>m chunks fail simultaneously).
        # Conservative upper bound: sum_{j=m+1}^{k+m} C(k+m, j) * p^j * (1-p)^(k+m-j)
        # plus correlated failure rate
        n = self.k + self.m
        p = chunk_annual_failure_rate
        prob = 0.0
        for j in range(self.m + 1, n + 1):
            prob += math.comb(n, j) * (p ** j) * ((1 - p) ** (n - j))
        return prob + correlated_failure_rate

def nines(prob: float) -> str:
    """Convert a loss probability to a durability 'nines' rating."""
    if prob <= 0:
        return "inf"
    durability = 1.0 - prob
    n = 0
    while durability >= 1 - 0.5 * (10 ** -(n + 1)) * 0.1:
        # iterate to count 9s roughly
        n += 1
        if n > 14:
            break
    # simpler: log10
    if prob >= 1:
        return "0"
    digits = -math.floor(math.log10(prob)) if prob > 0 else 99
    return f"~{digits} nines"

def report(name, cfg):
    print(f"--- {name} ---")
    print(f"  Storage overhead      : {cfg.storage_overhead():.2f}x")
    print(f"  Fault tolerance       : {cfg.fault_tolerance()} simultaneous failures")
    disk_fail = 0.01  # 1% annual disk failure rate
    loss_p = cfg.annual_data_loss_probability(disk_fail)
    print(f"  P(loss/year) @ 1% disk: {loss_p:.3e}")
    print(f"  Equivalent durability : {nines(loss_p)} nines")
    print()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("=== Durability Comparison ===\n")

    report("Replication RF=3", ReplicationConfig(rf=3))
    report("Replication RF=2", ReplicationConfig(rf=2))
    report("Erasure 10+4 (S3-like)", ErasureCodingConfig(k=10, m=4))
    report("Erasure 6+3 (HDFS-like)", ErasureCodingConfig(k=6, m=3))

    # Cost comparison at 1PB logical
    logical_pb = 1.0
    cost_per_pb_month = 23.0  # ~S3 standard us-east-1
    print("=== 1 PB stored, monthly storage cost ===")
    for name, oh in [
        ("RF=3", 3.0),
        ("RF=2", 2.0),
        ("Erasure 10+4", 14 / 10),
        ("Erasure 6+3", 9 / 6),
    ]:
        actual = logical_pb * oh
        monthly = actual * cost_per_pb_month
        print(f"  {name:15s}: stores {actual:.2f} PB, costs ${monthly*1000:,.0f}/mo")
```

quiz.question: What is the difference between durability and availability? Give an example of each.
options: The durability window is the gap between when a primary acknowledges a write to the client and when that write is replicated to the secondary.
Replication stores N identical copies; erasure coding splits data into k data chunks plus m parity chunks and stores k+m chunks across distinct failure domains,…
Silent data corruption is when stored data is altered without any error signal — the disk returns bytes, but they are not the bytes that were written.
Durability is "once written, the data survives forever"; availability is "the system is up and serving requests right now." A system can be durable but unavailable: an offline backup tape…
quiz.explanation: Durability is "once written, the data survives forever"; availability is "the system is up and serving requests right now." A system can be durable but unavailable: an offline backup tape in a vault is perfectly durable but the system cannot serve reads. A system can be available but not durable: an in-memory cache returns data instantly, but if the power fails, everything is lost.

quiz.question: Explain replication factor (RF) and quorum writes. Why does RF=3 with QUORUM give strong durability?
options: S3's 11 nines come from layered defenses, not a single mechanism.
The decision depends on workload characteristics and operational maturity, not on which is "better." Questions to ask: (1) What's the read/write ratio?
The likely cause is a partial infrastructure issue — a disk or rack failing within an AZ, causing S3 to fall back to slower reconstruction paths or to other AZs.
Replication factor RF is the number of replicas that store each piece of data — RF=3 means three independent copies.
quiz.explanation: Replication factor RF is the number of replicas that store each piece of data — RF=3 means three independent copies. Quorum write W is the number of replicas that must acknowledge a write before the client is told "done." With RF=3 and W=2 (QUORUM), the write is acked after any two of three replicas persist it.

quiz.question: Compare replication vs erasure coding. When does each win?
options: Push back on the framing: "cannot ever lose" is not an engineering target — it is impossible at finite cost.
S3's 11 nines come from layered defenses, not a single mechanism.
The decision depends on workload characteristics and operational maturity, not on which is "better." Questions to ask: (1) What's the read/write ratio?
Replication stores N identical copies; erasure coding splits data into k data chunks plus m parity chunks and stores k+m chunks across distinct failure domains,…
quiz.explanation: Replication stores N identical copies; erasure coding splits data into k data chunks plus m parity chunks and stores k+m chunks across distinct failure domains, tolerating loss of any m. Replication wins on simplicity, read latency (any replica can serve a read), and write latency (one replica ack suffices).

options: Durability is "once written, the data survives forever"; availability is "the system is up and serving requests right now." A system can be durable but unavailable: an offline backup tape…
The likely cause is a partial infrastructure issue — a disk or rack failing within an AZ, causing S3 to fall back to slower reconstruction paths or to other AZs.

quiz.explanation: Silent data corruption is when stored data is altered without any error signal — the disk returns bytes, but they are not the bytes that were written. Causes include bit rot on magnetic media, firmware bugs, controller errors, DRAM flips, and cosmic ray strikes on SSDs.

options: Silent data corruption is when stored data is altered without any error signal — the disk returns bytes, but they are not the bytes that were written.

quiz.explanation: The durability window is the gap between when a primary acknowledges a write to the client and when that write is replicated to the secondary. During this window, the data exists on only one node — if the primary crashes before replication completes, the write is lost even though the client was told it succeeded. This is the classic "data loss on failover" scenario.
